tasks.description: Create `person = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}`. Print the value for the key 'name'.
tasks.hint:
Access a dictionary value using its key in square brackets: `dictionary['key']`
`person['name']` → `'Alice'`
Note: if the key doesn't exist, you'll get a KeyError — use `.get()` to be safe.
tasks.walkthrough:
The key goes inside square brackets, in quotes because it's a string.
Python finds the matching entry and hands back its value.

tasks.description: Create `person = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}`. Add a key 'city' with value 'London'. Print the 'city' value.
tasks.hint:
Adding a new key is the same syntax as updating an existing one: `dict['key'] = value`
`person['city'] = 'London'` creates the key if it doesn't exist.
Then `print(person['city'])` → `'London'`
tasks.walkthrough:
Assigning to `person['city']` creates the key because it didn't exist yet.
Reading it back with the same square-bracket syntax gives London.

tasks.description: Create `scores = {'math': 90, 'english': 85, 'science': 92}`. Print each subject and score on a line like: 'math: 90'
tasks.hint:
`.items()` returns pairs of (key, value) you can unpack in a for loop.
`for subject, score in scores.items():` gives you both pieces each iteration.
`print(f'{subject}: {score}')` formats each line.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.items()` produces each pair as (key, value).
Writing two names after `for` unpacks each pair, so `subject` is the key and `score` is the value on every pass.
Dictionaries keep the order you added things in, so the output matches the order in the code.

tasks.description: Create `person = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}`. Try to get a key 'email' that doesn't exist. Use .get() so it returns 'not found' instead of crashing.
tasks.hint:
`dict['key']` raises a KeyError if the key doesn't exist — your program crashes.
`.get(key, default)` is safe — it returns the default if the key is missing.
`person.get('email', 'not found')` → `'not found'` without any error.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.get()` takes the key to look for and a fallback to return if it's missing.
There's no email key, so the fallback string is returned and printed. No crash.

tasks.description: Create `person = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25, 'city': 'London'}`. Print True if 'age' is a key, False if not.
tasks.hint:
The `in` keyword checks dictionary KEYS (not values): `'age' in person`
This returns `True` because 'age' exists as a key.
`print('age' in person)` prints the boolean result directly.
tasks.walkthrough:
`in` on a dictionary checks whether the key exists.
'age' is one of the keys, so the result is `True`.

tasks.description: Create `inventory = {'apples': 5, 'bananas': 3}`. Update apples to 10, then print the total count of all items (sum of all values).
tasks.hint:
Update: `inventory['apples'] = 10` — same syntax as creating a new key.
`.values()` returns all the values: `inventory.values()` → `dict_values([10, 3])`
`sum(inventory.values())` adds them all up → `13`
tasks.walkthrough:
Assigning to an existing key replaces its value, so apples goes from 5 to 10.
`.values()` gives just the numbers, and `sum()` adds them: 10 + 3 = 13.

tasks.description: Create `data = {'x': 1, 'y': 2, 'z': 3}`. Print the number of key-value pairs in the dictionary.
tasks.hint:
`len()` works on dictionaries — it counts the number of key-value pairs.
`len({'x': 1, 'y': 2, 'z': 3})` → `3`
It counts keys (not values), so each key-value pair counts as one.
tasks.walkthrough:
`len()` on a dictionary counts the key-value pairs.
Three keys means three pairs, so the answer is 3.

lesson.intro:
A list finds things by position. A dictionary finds things by name. If you've ever
used a contacts app, that's a dictionary: you look up "Alice" and get her number.
Dictionaries store pairs of a key and a value.

sections.heading: Keys and values
sections.body:
Curly braces, and each entry is `key: value`. Keys are usually strings.
To look something up, put the key in square brackets after the name,
the same way you'd use a position with a list.

sections.heading: Adding and changing entries
sections.body:
Assigning to a key that doesn't exist creates it. Assigning to one that
does exist overwrites the value. Same syntax for both.

sections.heading: Looking up a key that might not exist
sections.body:
`person['email']` crashes with a KeyError if there's no such key.
`person.get('email', 'not found')` returns the fallback instead. Use `.get()`
whenever you're not sure the key is there.

To just check, `'email' in person` gives `True` or `False`. Note that `in`
looks at the keys, not the values.
sections.code:
person = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}
print(person.get('email', 'not found'))
print('age' in person)
print('Alice' in person)

sections.heading: Looping over a dictionary
sections.body:
`.items()` gives you each key and value together, which you can unpack into
two loop variables. There's also `.keys()` and `.values()` if you only need
one side.

watch_out: Keys are case-sensitive and exact. `person['Name']` and `person['name']` are different keys.
`'1'` and `1` are different keys. Text and numbers don't mix here either.
`x in my_dict` checks keys. To check values, use `x in my_dict.values()`.
Square-bracket lookup on a missing key crashes. Reach for `.get()` when in doubt.
